The search turned up a long-standing WebKit discrepancy, though not a confirmed current fix.

- **The bug report:** WebKit bug 201591 was filed in 2019 and argues that Safari's handling of `'self'` doesn't follow the spec. Under the spec, `'self'` should also cover `ws:`/`wss:` on the same host and port. The reporter saw Safari block a same-host `wss://` connection. The bug is now marked resolved as a duplicate of bug 235873. A commenter reported in 2021 that it was still not fixed in Safari 14. I couldn't find the fix status for bug 235873, so I can't say whether current Safari versions behave correctly.
- **Spec behavior:** The W3C issue that prompted this shows the spec deliberately does not treat `'self'` as matching WebSockets. A maintainer wrote that this is the specified behavior at the time. MDN notes that connect-src 'self' does not resolve to websocket schemes in all browsers, so the behavior varies across browsers.
- **Workaround in practice:** Projects have added explicit WebSocket sources. One OpenBMC commit added 'wss:' to connect-src directive in CSP to fix Safari console errors for WebSocket connections.

For a practical fix, list the WebSocket scheme explicitly (for example `connect-src 'self' wss:`) rather than relying on `'self'`, and test in current Safari, since I couldn't verify whether the bug is fixed in recent releases.

The search didn't turn up a page that directly matches the exact error you described (a certificate error causing Chrome to reject a Secure cookie with "origin not set"). The results cover related Secure-cookie behavior instead.

- **Secure cookies from insecure origins:** A draft spec on Secure cookies notes that non-secure origins can historically set cookies that get delivered to secure origins. Due to historical accident, non-secure origins can set cookies which will be delivered to secure connections. Per the same post, a cookie from an insecure scheme should not overwrite an existing Secure cookie with the same name and domain match.
- **Chrome's localhost handling:** A GitHub discussion compares browsers. Chrome accepts the Secure attribute on cookies over localhost, but does not support __Host- or __Secure- prefixed cookies there, while Firefox supports both.
- **Chrome's trustworthy-origin warnings:** A Chromium commit adds warnings for Secure cookies set or accessed from trustworthy but non-cryptographic URLs. Per the commit, cookies that aren't allowed to be set because the URL isn't trustworthy get excluded by the cookie store.
- **Secure cookies not overwritten over HTTP:** A blog post reports that Chrome 71 and Firefox 64 prevent a secure cookie from being overwritten on plain http.
- **Certificate errors and origins:** A Chromium developer explains that Chrome uses interstitial warnings partly to keep the browser from sending cookies to an impostor origin. This suggests that a certificate error can block the origin from being treated as trustworthy, which may explain Secure cookies being dropped.

For the exact error, I'd suggest searching Chromium bug tracker or Stack Overflow with terms like "cookie rejected" plus "net::ERR_CERT" or "SameSite/Secure" and checking DevTools' Issues tab for the specific cookie-blocking reason.

The search turned up no Apple documentation on this. The only direct evidence is an older bug report, and it's dated.

- **Observed behavior (2016):** A blogger reported that Safari on iOS appeared to keep a certificate bypass indefinitely. They had tested whether it expired after a new window or a set time period, and it did not seem to. As far as I can tell the cert bypass is remembered indefinitely.
- **Suggested policy:** The same author pointed to a research paper by Weinberger and Felt that recommends certificate exceptions expire after one week. We think cert exceptions should expire after 1 week
- **Certificate lifetime limits:** Apple's trust rules are a separate issue. For certificates issued from iOS 13 and macOS 10.15 onward, TLS server certificates must have a validity period of 825 days or fewer. A 2020 test on a 10-year self-signed cert showed Safari on macOS 10.13 still let the user proceed after prompting to change trust settings, while the newer macOS 10.15 blocked bypassing the warning entirely. (That report is about macOS, not iOS.) With macos 10.13 (high sierra), chrome will allow you to ignore the check and continue on, but safari will warn after clicking "visit this website".

Bottom line: the only observation I found says the exception persists indefinitely, and it's from 2016. I couldn't confirm whether current iOS versions behave the same way, and I found no Apple documentation on exception expiry. Testing on a current iOS device would be the reliable way to check.

Links: [{"title":"show bug","url":"https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=23576"},{"title":"[Bug 23576] New: Clarify what to do when received null value subprotocol in reply to non-empty subprotocol","url":"https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-webapps/2013OctDec/0229.html"},{"title":"github.com","url":"https://github.com/gobwas/ws/issues/81"},{"title":"oneuptime.com","url":"https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-24-websocket-protocol-error/view"},{"title":"ASTERISK 22441","url":"https://issues-archive.asterisk.org/ASTERISK-22441"},{"title":"www.rfc-editor.org","url":"https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc6455.html"},{"title":"WebKit Bugzilla","url":"https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=271122"},{"title":"www2.greenbytes.de","url":"https://www2.greenbytes.de/tech/specs/rfc6455.pdf"},{"title":"greenbytes.de","url":"https://greenbytes.de/tech/specs/rfc6455.pdf"}]

The search turned up one clear answer and one gap in RFC 6455.

**The case RFC 6455 covers:** If the server's response names a subprotocol the client did not request, the client must fail the connection. A gobwas/ws GitHub discussion quotes the RFC's wording, which uses the term "MUST Fail the WebSocket Connection" (If the response includes a Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header field and this header field indicates the use of a subprotocol that was not present in the client's handshake). An Asterisk bug report makes the same point from the spec (the spec says the client MUST Fail the WebSocket Connection if the client omits the protocol but the server supplies one in its response).

**The case your query asks about (client offered subprotocols, server returns none):** RFC 6455 does not clearly require failure here. A W3C bug report states that RFC 6455 itself doesn't require a client to abort connection establishment. That report also notes that the RFC specifies the WebSocket protocol layer to fail on two cases but not the case where the client requested subprotocols and the server sent none. The report proposed explicit language for this case, which the WHATWG WebSocket standard appears to have adopted. A WebKit bug discussion quotes it as: If protocols is not the empty list and extracting header list values given Sec-WebSocket-Protocol and response's header list results in null, failure, or the empty byte sequence, then fail the WebSocket connection.

**Practical takeaway:** Under RFC 6455 alone, a client that offered subprotocols and received none is not explicitly required to fail. Under the WHATWG standard, browsers should fail the connection in that case. Server-side libraries may accept such a handshake, so a server that requires a specific subprotocol has to enforce that check itself. One GitHub user found exactly this: their server accepted connections when the client omitted the header, because the subprotocol check was never called.

I did not open the RFC or WHATWG text directly. The quotes above come from secondary sources (bug reports and issue threads), so check the current RFC 6455 text and the WHATWG WebSocket standard before relying on the exact wording.

The results agree that six connections per host is the common browser limit for HTTP/1.1, but they are mostly older sources. None of them cover speculative preconnect or socket pool internals.

- **The RFC basis:** The HTTP/1.1 spec once gave a numeric cap of two connections per server. RFC 7230 later dropped specific numbers, calling them impractical and advising conservatism when opening multiple connections.
- **Browser values, 2008:** Steve Souders' roundup listed Opera and Safari at 4 connections per server, and it notes that Chrome 4+ used 6 connections for HTTP/1.1.
- **Newer vendor docs:** A Diffusion guide says Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Opera, iOS and Android each allow 6 connections per host, and that the limit applies per browser and not per browser tab.
- **Per-host versus total:** One table lists Chrome 19 at 6 per host and 40 total. Another cites Safari 7.0.1 at 6 per hostname and 17 total. Modern browsers support 6-13 connections per hostname, according to a tutorial, though that source is low-authority.
- **Configuration:** Firefox exposes the per-server limit as a preference, network.http.max-persistent-connections-per-server, per a forum post.

Gaps: nothing here confirms current Chrome or Safari values, and nothing addresses speculative preconnect or socket-pool behaviour. Those would need Chromium or WebKit source documentation.

**1. Sec-WebSocket-Protocol check (§2.2, step 11.2)**

The step reads: "If protocols is not the empty list and extracting header list values given `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`" followed by "results in null, failure, or the empty byte sequence, then fail the WebSocket connection."

The spec adds that this check differs from the RFC 6455 check. The RFC only rejects a subprotocol the server selected that the client didn't request. This step rejects the case where the client requested subprotocols and the server acknowledged none.

**2. Cookies and credentials (§2.2, step 2)**

The handshake request is created with credentials mode "`include`", and the spec says that "This way CSP, cookies, HSTS, and other Fetch-related protocols are handled in a single location." The document doesn't spell out cookie details beyond this, so those details live in the Fetch Standard.

**3. Userinfo and fragments**

- **Fragments:** Rejected. The constructor throws a SyntaxError if the parsed URL's fragment is non-null, and the spec notes that "URLs with fragments will always cause such an exception."
- **Userinfo:** The document doesn't mention it. The connection algorithm uses only the host, port, path, and query, so the spec doesn't say how userinfo is handled.

The search covered the service worker half of your question but not the cookie half.

**Service worker registration failure:** A self-signed certificate is the usual cause. MSW's docs explain that the browser will not trust your self-signed certificate, so it blocks the Service Worker registration attempt. The resulting error is typically "An SSL certificate error occurred when fetching the script."

**Workarounds mentioned in the results:**
- MSW's guide suggests enabling the unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure flag at chrome://flags and entering your localhost origin, and says that if you hit certificate fetching or validation issues, you should set the ignore-certificate-errors flag to "Enabled".
- A Chromium-extensions discussion notes that individual users can ignore certificate errors by launching Chrome with the --ignore-certificate-errors flag.
- A Chromium bug report from 2015 says some users found the localhost-specific flags didn't help, so results may vary by Chrome version. That thread is old and I couldn't confirm its current status.

**Secure context:** One source notes that the page and service worker script must be served in a secure context, which requires HTTPS with a trusted certificate. That lines up with your `isSecureContext` check: an untrusted certificate typically leaves the page non-secure for this purpose.

**Cookies (HttpOnly/Secure):** Nothing in these results addresses whether Secure or HttpOnly cookies are still set under a bypassed certificate error. That would need a separate search, or testing directly in DevTools (Application → Cookies) with the bypass in place.

The search results consistently say that Chrome 58 stopped using the Common Name field to validate certificates and now relies only on the Subject Alternative Name extension.

- **The change:** One write-up describes Chrome 58 as dropping CN-based validation in favor of SAN-only checks. Beginning with Chrome 58, the Chrome browser no longer uses the Common Name (CN) field to validate an SSL certificate. Instead, it only uses the Subject Alternative Name field. Chrome's own Google support article, which the forum posts cite, is the primary reference, but I did not retrieve its text.
- **Why it's contentious:** The same blog argues this conflicts with RFC 2828, which treats CN as a fallback only when no dNSName SAN exists, and it notes that most single name certificates and some wildcard certificates only have a Common Name and don't have use Subject Alternative Names.
- **The error:** Certificates without a matching SAN trigger the following (incorrect) error, which the blog identifies as NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID [missing_subjectAltName]. A Chromium developer post on the change says all common names are now ignored for this error code. Newer Chrome builds show [missing_subjectAltName] in the details on the Certificate Error page, which helps confirm the cause.
- **The fix:** Regenerate the certificate with a SAN entry. For a Windows internal CA, the blog describes doing this through the Certificates MMC. For OpenSSL, one forum user added SAN settings to the config file's v3_req section. A commenter also noted that the CA's common name doesn't matter, but the certificate must include the hostname or IP in the SAN field. Let's Encrypt certificates already include this.
- **Related:** One source notes that this follows a similar change in Firefox 48.

The search didn't return the chromium.org policy page itself. The results point to the policy being disabled by default in Chrome 58 and then removed around Chrome 65 or 66, with sources disagreeing on the exact version.

- **Origin:** A Chromium commit disabled commonName matching by default and added this enterprise policy for certificates that chain to local trust anchors. Matching the commonName has been deprecated for nearly 20 years, as it's a fallback path for certificates that don't have a subjectAltName. Disable the matching by default, but introduce an enterprise policy that allows it to be enabled for certificates that chain to local trust anchors.
- **Removal version:** Vendor guidance says the workaround stops at Chrome 65. Epson's FAQ states this is a work-around that will not function beyond version 65 of Google Chrome, and should only be used a temporary fix. RSA's notes say it is only good for a year or until Chrome 65 comes out. A Microsoft Edge engineer, however, wrote that the policy EnableCommonNameFallbackForLocalAnchors was removed in Chrome 66. So 65 and 66 both appear in sources, and I couldn't confirm which is correct from these results.
- **Fix:** The Microsoft engineer advised that you'll need to update the certificate generator such that it generates certificates containing SubjectAltNames.

Apple's current support guidance says you can scan a QR code with the built-in Camera app or the Code Scanner control. Open the Camera app from the Home Screen, Lock Screen, or Control Center, or use the Camera Control on supported models. Holding the device steady over the code brings it into view, and then you tap the link to open the content. Apple's page also explains that the Code Scanner can be added to Control Center by touching and holding the background, tapping Add a Control, and selecting the Scan Code control.

Older Apple guidance described the same flow with a notification step. The device recognizes the code and shows a notification, and tapping that notification opens the linked page.

Some users in Apple's community forums reported that the camera never recognized a particular code, even though other codes worked. One suggested workaround was to keep the iPhone in portrait mode and try the code on another screen. Apple's official instructions are the more reliable reference.

content.content:
The thread says the **NSURLSession WebSocket** experimental feature is **enabled by default on iOS 15 and macOS Monterey**. The original poster found that disabling it made WebSocket work again. They also found that with the feature on, sending messages over **84 bytes** broke the connection, while smaller messages worked.

There is **no Apple engineer reply** in the content. The only reply is from user XFox, who suggested that WebKit Bugzilla [Bug 230962](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=230962), "WebSocket connection terminated when server sends junk," might be related. The thread has no comments and no confirmed root cause or fix.

input.content:
# Facts for issue #230 (web control surface)

No spike was run. Every open question left is about a real browser on a device, or needs a person's click on a warning page. None is runnable here.

## Settled

- The wire `SessionView` has no excerpt field. It carries `card`, `waiting` and `waiting_reason`, but no `last_message`. — `control/src/lib.rs:637-688`. `last_message` is parsed from the Stop hook (`src/adapters/hooks.rs:71,196`, `src/ports/events.rs:24`) but never reaches a view. The headset shows `waitingReason` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:745`). So the "one-line excerpt the card shows" needs an additive field, or the page drops it.
- `last-response` for any session that is not a Claude Code session answers `400` with code `no_conversation` ("only a Claude Code session has a conversation"). A Claude Code session with no handle yet gets the same code with "has not started a conversation yet". — `src/app.rs:1869-1886`.
- `screen` on a session that is not running answers `400 failed` "not running". — `src/app.rs:1863-1866`.
- No remote route logs `request.query`. `refuse` logs method and path (`src/app.rs:3762-3766`), and `pair` logs the device name and scope (`:3666-3670`). The adapter's only log line is the connection error (`src/adapters/remote.rs:714`). `RemoteRequest` derives `Debug` with `query` in it (`src/adapters/remote.rs:358-371`), so a future `{request:?}` would leak the code.
- The certificate as made today has no SAN, no EKU and no basicConstraints. It has NotBefore 1975-01-01 and NotAfter 4096-01-01. — `src/adapters/remote.rs:101-110`; `~/.cargo/registry/src/*/rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:82-96`.
- Apple: for every TLS server certificate on iOS 13+/macOS 10.15+, the name must be in the SAN, and "DNS names in the CommonName … are no longer trusted". "Connections to TLS servers violating these new requirements will fail." Since iOS 13, the 825-day limit and the `serverAuth` EKU apply only to certificates whose NotBefore is after 2019-07-01. Today's NotBefore of 1975 falls outside both, so the missing SAN is the one Apple rule today's certificate breaks. — https://support.apple.com/103769 (published 2023-11-06). Queries: "Apple requirements for trusted certificates iOS 13 macOS 10.15 subjectAltName 825 days".
- Apple's 398-day limit applies only to certificates from preinstalled roots. It "will not affect certificates issued from user-added or administrator-added Root CAs". — https://support.apple.com/102028 (2023-08-21). Same query.
- Chrome has ignored the commonName since Chrome 58. A certificate with no SAN fails name matching with `NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID`. The enterprise fallback policy was removed in 65/66. — Chromium commit "Disable commonName matching for certificates", https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/b166233e0fb8edd9fd4e67bc4a6bfb8e35b79144. Queries: "Chrome 58 remove support for commonName matching … ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID"; "chromium.org EnableCommonNameFallbackForLocalAnchors policy removed Chrome 65 subjectAltName". Corollary: a certificate reissued over the **same key** with an IP SAN keeps every SPKI pin (the pin is over the key, `src/adapters/remote.rs:111`).
- iOS: a certificate from a manually installed profile is not trusted for TLS until the user turns it on under Settings › General › About › Certificate Trust Settings, "Enable full trust for root certificates". Profiles from MDM or Configurator are trusted automatically. — https://support.apple.com/102390. Query: "iOS Certificate Trust Settings full trust root certificates only manually installed profile Apple support". The page names root certificates only. Whether a leaf with no basicConstraints is listed there is under Unresolved.
- WHATWG WebSockets: a browser that offered `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` values fails the connection unless the 101 echoes one of them. — https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ §2.2 step 11.2. Queries: "RFC 6455 Sec-WebSocket-Protocol server response does not include subprotocol client must fail". Today's `respond_upgrade` echoes none (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`, per the investigation).
- The token is URL-safe base64 with no padding (`src/adapters/remote.rs:337-341`). Every character is a `tchar`, so it is a legal subprotocol value.
- The WebSocket handshake is fetched with credentials mode `include`, so cookies for the origin ride on the upgrade the same way they ride on `fetch`. A URL with a fragment throws. — https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ §2.2 step 2.
- CSP `'self'` and `wss:`: the spec issue left `'self'` not matching WebSocket schemes. MDN says "connect-src 'self' does not resolve to websocket schemes in all browsers". WebKit bug 201591 (Safari blocked same-host `wss:` under `'self'`) was closed as a duplicate of 235873, "CSP: Improve compatibility of source matching", which was fixed in r292266 (2022-04-02). — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/connect-src, https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=235873. Query: "CSP connect-src 'self' WebSocket wss Safari WebKit bug 'self' does not match ws". Naming the origin explicitly, as `connect-src 'self' wss://<host>:<port>` (the host the page was loaded from), works on every engine whatever the version. OpenBMC ships that workaround (https://gerrit.openbmc.org/plugins/gitiles/openbmc/phosphor-webui/+/0824e49e0f91b1d4ff6d07ec81927fb410ccd29e%5E%21).
- iOS Camera: scanning a URL shows a link, and the user taps it to open the page in Safari. Nothing opens without the tap. — https://support.apple.com/102680. Query: "Apple support scan a QR code with iPhone camera tap the link that appears".

## Unresolved

- **Is there a click-through on iOS Safari for an IP URL whose certificate has no SAN?** Apple says such connections "will fail" (103769). That text is about trust, not the warning page. One forum post (bensoftware) and ThinLinc's docs ("cannot connect through an IP address" in Safari) are leads only. Queries: "Safari iOS "This Connection Is Not Private" self-signed certificate IP address no subjectAltName "visit this website" not shown". **The plan must build anyway**: reissue the certificate over the same key with an `iPAddress` SAN for each served address, and a `dNSName` for the `.local` name if the page is offered by name. Add EKU `serverAuth`, and keep a pre-2019 NotBefore or a validity of 825 days or less. This is the only form that both Apple and Chrome accept as name-matching. Reissue when `local_address()` changes. If the answer is favourable, nothing more is needed. If it is unfavourable, the SAN is what fixes it.
- **Does `wss://` work on iOS Safari after a click-through exception?** WebKit bug 41419 is still NEW (last comment 2014, rdar 17898486), and a 2011 webkit-dev thread says Safari did not extend an https exception to wss. Cockpit ships a documented workaround: Safari's WebSocket "does not support the WebSocket Secure sessions" with a self-signed certificate "even when they are manually marked as trusted", and it enables "NSURLSession WebSocket" (https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari, undated). The Apple developer forum (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/694113) says NSURLSession WebSocket became the default in iOS 15. No source says whether that fixes the exception case on current iOS. Queries: "Safari iOS self-signed certificate WebSocket wss fails after accepting certificate warning WebKit bug"; "Safari iOS 17 accept self-signed certificate then WebSocket wss connection fails …"; "Safari 15 NSURLSession WebSocket enabled by default release notes WebKit". **The plan must build anyway**: the page falls back to polling the REST reads by revision when the events socket fails to open or closes at once, and says it is polling. If wss works, the fallback stays dormant.
- **Can a self-signed leaf be fully trusted on iOS, or only a root?** Apple's page names only roots (102390). Queries as above. **Build to work in both cases**: if the plan offers a certificate download, the certificate has `basicConstraints CA:TRUE` with the same key, or the host makes a separate local CA. Otherwise the click-through is the trust step. The first is a design choice for the planner.
- **Are `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookies stored and sent after a certificate exception (Chrome, Safari), and kept across restarts on an IP host?** No source found. A 2014 Chromium thread (Palmer, public-webappsec 2014Dec/0131) is a lead only. Queries: "Chrome secure cookie certificate error origin not set …"; "Chromium cookies not stored or not persisted on HTTPS page with certificate error interstitial proceed"; "Chrome certificate error bypass page isSecureContext service worker … cookies HttpOnly Secure still set" (extended). **Works in both cases**: carry the token as a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value, with the 101 echoing a fixed protocol name, and as a bearer header on `fetch`. This needs no cookie store. A cookie is an addition the plan may make only if the owner's run shows it is kept.
- **How long does iOS Safari keep a certificate exception?** One 2016 blog (kingant.net) observed it lasting "indefinitely". Nothing current. Query: "iOS Safari self-signed certificate exception how long remembered …". **Build anyway**: the page treats a failed load as needing the warning again. The dialog sentence says the warning may come back.
- **How many connections does a first page load open?** Older sources say 6 per host for HTTP/1.1 (Steve Souders' 2008 roundup; Diffusion docs). Nothing current covers speculative preconnect. Query: "browser maximum persistent connections per host HTTP/1.1 six Chrome Safari speculative preconnect socket pool". **Build anyway**: a page load must not starve the four unauthenticated slots (`src/adapters/remote.rs:567`). Either static replies close the connection (`Connection: close`), or static paths count against a separate bound. The plan picks which.
- **Does the scanned URL with the code reach Safari history or another record before `replaceState`?** No source found. The camera requires a tap (Settled). **Build anyway**: the code is single-use and bounded by the window (`src/core/remote.rs:46-71`), and the page strips the query first.
- **Does the subprotocol value appear in Web Inspector?** No source found. Same query family as above. It is the owner's own device either way, and the token is already readable by the page's script under this choice.

## For the owner

- On your iPhone/iPad (state the iOS version): with a SAN'd certificate, does Safari show "visit this website" for `https://<ip>:43187/`, and after you accept, do the page and the events socket both work? If yes, the click-through is the trust step. If the socket fails, the REST-polling fallback carries the page. The fallback works in both cases.
- On the same device, after you accept: does a cookie set by `/pair` survive closing Safari? If yes, the plan may add a cookie. If no, the subprotocol and stored token stay. The subprotocol works in both cases.
- Does your network let the phone reach the Mac on port 43187 (no client isolation)? If yes, proceed. If no, nothing in this tree can fix it, and the acceptance run moves to another network.

It carries `card`, `waiting` and `waiting_reason`, but no `last_message`. — `control/src/lib.rs:637-688`. `last_message` is parsed from the Stop hook (`src/adapters/hooks.rs:71,196`, `src/ports/events.rs:24`) but never reaches a view. The headset shows `waitingReason` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:745`). So the "one-line excerpt the card shows" needs an additive field, or the page drops it.
- `last-response` for any session that is not a Claude Code session answers `400` with code `no_conversation` ("only a Claude Code session has a conversation"). A Claude Code session with no handle yet gets the same code with "has not started a conversation yet". — `src/app.rs:1869-1886`.
- `screen` on a session that is not running answers `400 failed` "not running". — `src/app.rs:1863-1866`.
- No remote route logs `request.query`. `refuse` logs method and path (`src/app.rs:3762-3766`), and `pair` logs the device name and scope (`:3666-3670`). The adapter's only log line is the connection error (`src/adapters/remote.rs:714`). `RemoteRequest` derives `Debug` with `query` in it (`src/adapters/remote.rs:358-371`), so a future `{request:?}` would leak the code.
- The certificate as made today has no SAN, no EKU and no basicConstraints. It has NotBefore 1975-01-01 and NotAfter 4096-01-01. — `src/adapters/remote.rs:101-110`; `~/.cargo/registry/src/*/rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:82-96`.
- Apple: for every TLS server certificate on iOS 13+/macOS 10.15+, the name must be in the SAN, and "DNS names in the CommonName … are no longer trusted". "Connections to TLS servers violating these new requirements will fail." Since iOS 13, the 825-day limit and the `serverAuth` EKU apply only to certificates whose NotBefore is after 2019-07-01. Today's NotBefore of 1975 falls outside both, so the missing SAN is the one Apple rule today's certificate breaks. — https://support.apple.com/103769 (published 2023-11-06). Queries: "Apple requirements for trusted certificates iOS 13 macOS 10.15 subjectAltName 825 days".
- Apple's 398-day limit applies only to certificates from preinstalled roots. It "will not affect certificates issued from user-added or administrator-added Root CAs". — https://support.apple.com/102028 (2023-08-21). Same query.
- Chrome has ignored the commonName since Chrome 58. A certificate with no SAN fails name matching with `NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID`. The enterprise fallback policy was removed in 65/66. — Chromium commit "Disable commonName matching for certificates", https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/b166233e0fb8edd9fd4e67bc4a6bfb8e35b79144. Queries: "Chrome 58 remove support for commonName matching … ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID"; "chromium.org EnableCommonNameFallbackForLocalAnchors policy removed Chrome 65 subjectAltName". Corollary: a certificate reissued over the **same key** with an IP SAN keeps every SPKI pin (the pin is over the key, `src/adapters/remote.rs:111`).
- iOS: a certificate from a manually installed profile is not trusted for TLS until the user turns it on under Settings › General › About › Certificate Trust Settings, "Enable full trust for root certificates". Profiles from MDM or Configurator are trusted automatically. — https://support.apple.com/102390. Query: "iOS Certificate Trust Settings full trust root certificates only manually installed profile Apple support". The page names root certificates only. Whether a leaf with no basicConstraints is listed there is under Unresolved.
- WHATWG WebSockets: a browser that offered `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` values fails the connection unless the 101 echoes one of them. — https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ §2.2 step 11.2. Queries: "RFC 6455 Sec-WebSocket-Protocol server response does not include subprotocol client must fail". Today's `respond_upgrade` echoes none (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`, per the investigation).
- The token is URL-safe base64 with no padding (`src/adapters/remote.rs:337-341`). Every character is a `tchar`, so it is a legal subprotocol value.
- The WebSocket handshake is fetched with credentials mode `include`, so cookies for the origin ride on the upgrade the same way they ride on `fetch`. A URL with a fragment throws. — https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ §2.2 step 2.
- CSP `'self'` and `wss:`: the spec issue left `'self'` not matching WebSocket schemes. MDN says "connect-src 'self' does not resolve to websocket schemes in all browsers". WebKit bug 201591 (Safari blocked same-host `wss:` under `'self'`) was closed as a duplicate of 235873, "CSP: Improve compatibility of source matching", which was fixed in r292266 (2022-04-02). — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/connect-src, https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=235873. Query: "CSP connect-src 'self' WebSocket wss Safari WebKit bug 'self' does not match ws". Naming the origin explicitly, as `connect-src 'self' wss://<host>:<port>` (the host the page was loaded from), works on every engine whatever the version. OpenBMC ships that workaround (https://gerrit.openbmc.org/plugins/gitiles/openbmc/phosphor-webui/+/0824e49e0f91b1d4ff6d07ec81927fb410ccd29e%5E%21).
- iOS Camera: scanning a URL shows a link, and the user taps it to open the page in Safari. Nothing opens without the tap. — https://support.apple.com/102680. Query: "Apple support scan a QR code with iPhone camera tap the link that appears".

## Unresolved

- **Is there a click-through on iOS Safari for an IP URL whose certificate has no SAN?** Apple says such connections "will fail" (103769). That text is about trust, not the warning page. One forum post (bensoftware) and ThinLinc's docs ("cannot connect through an IP address" in Safari) are leads only. Queries: "Safari iOS "This Connection Is Not Private" self-signed certificate IP address no subjectAltName "visit this website" not shown". **The plan must build anyway**: reissue the certificate over the same key with an `iPAddress` SAN for each served address, and a `dNSName` for the `.local` name if the page is offered by name. Add EKU `serverAuth`, and keep a pre-2019 NotBefore or a validity of 825 days or less. This is the only form that both Apple and Chrome accept as name-matching. Reissue when `local_address()` changes. If the answer is favourable, nothing more is needed. If it is unfavourable, the SAN is what fixes it.
- **Does `wss://` work on iOS Safari after a click-through exception?** WebKit bug 41419 is still NEW (last comment 2014, rdar 17898486), and a 2011 webkit-dev thread says Safari did not extend an https exception to wss. Cockpit ships a documented workaround: Safari's WebSocket "does not support the WebSocket Secure sessions" with a self-signed certificate "even when they are manually marked as trusted", and it enables "NSURLSession WebSocket" (https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari, undated). The Apple developer forum (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/694113) says NSURLSession WebSocket became the default in iOS 15. No source says whether that fixes the exception case on current iOS. Queries: "Safari iOS self-signed certificate WebSocket wss fails after accepting certificate warning WebKit bug"; "Safari iOS 17 accept self-signed certificate then WebSocket wss connection fails …"; "Safari 15 NSURLSession WebSocket enabled by default release notes WebKit". **The plan must build anyway**: the page falls back to polling the REST reads by revision when the events socket fails to open or closes at once, and says it is polling. If wss works, the fallback stays dormant.
- **Can a self-signed leaf be fully trusted on iOS, or only a root?** Apple's page names only roots (102390). Queries as above. **Build to work in both cases**: if the plan offers a certificate download, the certificate has `basicConstraints CA:TRUE` with the same key, or the host makes a separate local CA. Otherwise the click-through is the trust step. The first is a design choice for the planner.
- **Are `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookies stored and sent after a certificate exception (Chrome, Safari), and kept across restarts on an IP host?** No source found. A 2014 Chromium thread (Palmer, public-webappsec 2014Dec/0131) is a lead only. Queries: "Chrome secure cookie certificate error origin not set …"; "Chromium cookies not stored or not persisted on HTTPS page with certificate error interstitial proceed"; "Chrome certificate error bypass page isSecureContext service worker … cookies HttpOnly Secure still set" (extended). **Works in both cases**: carry the token as a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value, with the 101 echoing a fixed protocol name, and as a bearer header on `fetch`. This needs no cookie store. A cookie is an addition the plan may make only if the owner's run shows it is kept.
- **How long does iOS Safari keep a certificate exception?** One 2016 blog (kingant.net) observed it lasting "indefinitely". Nothing current. Query: "iOS Safari self-signed certificate exception how long remembered …". **Build anyway**: the page treats a failed load as needing the warning again. The dialog sentence says the warning may come back.
- **How many connections does a first page load open?** Older sources say 6 per host for HTTP/1.1 (Steve Souders' 2008 roundup; Diffusion docs). Nothing current covers speculative preconnect. Query: "browser maximum persistent connections per host HTTP/1.1 six Chrome Safari speculative preconnect socket pool". **Build anyway**: a page load must not starve the four unauthenticated slots (`src/adapters/remote.rs:567`). Either static replies close the connection (`Connection: close`), or static paths count against a separate bound. The plan picks which.
- **Does the scanned URL with the code reach Safari history or another record before `replaceState`?** No source found. The camera requires a tap (Settled). **Build anyway**: the code is single-use and bounded by the window (`src/core/remote.rs:46-71`), and the page strips the query first.
- **Does the subprotocol value appear in Web Inspector?** No source found. Same query family as above. It is the owner's own device either way, and the token is already readable by the page's script under this choice.

## For the owner

- On your iPhone/iPad (state the iOS version): with a SAN'd certificate, does Safari show "visit this website" for `https://<ip>:43187/`, and after you accept, do the page and the events socket both work? If yes, the click-through is the trust step. If the socket fails, the REST-polling fallback carries the page. The fallback works in both cases.
- On the same device, after you accept: does a cookie set by `/pair` survive closing Safari? If yes, the plan may add a cookie. If no, the subprotocol and stored token stay. The subprotocol works in both cases.
- Does your network let the phone reach the Mac on port 43187 (no client isolation)? If yes, proceed. If no, nothing in this tree can fix it, and the acceptance run moves to another network.

I wrote the facts file to `/Users/sbgragent/Library/Application Support/Dispatch/tickets/91423ada/facts/1/repo/facts.md` (just under 1500 words). I ran no spike: every question still open needs a phone or a person clicking through a certificate warning. Nothing was committed and git status is empty.

**Settled:**
- **The card excerpt isn't sent.** The session view the API sends has no excerpt field (`control/src/lib.rs:637-688`). `last_message` is read from the Stop hook but never reaches the API. The plan needs to add a field or leave the excerpt out.
- **Error codes the page will see.** `last-response` on anything but a Claude Code session answers `400 no_conversation`. `screen` on a stopped session answers `400 failed`.
- **The pairing code isn't logged.** No remote route logs the query string. But the request type's debug output includes it, so a future `{request:?}` would log the code.
- **The certificate has a name problem.** Today's certificate has no subjectAltName, which is where browsers look for the host's name or address. Apple and Chrome both ignore the CN, which is where today's certificate puts its name. Its NotBefore date is 1975, so Apple's 825-day and EKU rules (which only cover certificates issued after July 2019) don't apply to it. The missing subjectAltName is the one rule it breaks. A certificate reissued over the same key with an IP-address entry keeps every native client's pin.
- **iOS manual trust.** The "full trust" switch is described for root certificates only.
- **Token in the WebSocket handshake.** A browser fails the socket if the server doesn't echo back an offered `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value. The token's characters are all legal in that header.
- **CSP.** Old Safari didn't let `connect-src 'self'` cover `wss:`. WebKit fixed it in 2022; naming `wss:` explicitly works in every browser regardless.
- **iOS Camera.** Scanning a URL shows a link; nothing opens until the user taps it.

**Unresolved.** Each one names what the plan must build regardless of the answer:
- **Click-through for an IP address with no subjectAltName on iOS:** reissue the certificate with an IP-address entry anyway.
- **`wss://` after a click-through on iOS:** a WebKit bug about it (41419) is still open, and Cockpit documents the failure. The page needs a fallback that polls the REST reads when the socket fails.
- **Cookies after a certificate exception:** no source found. A token sent in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` works without a cookie store, so it works either way.
- **Connections per page load:** probably six, which is more than the four unauthenticated slots. Static replies must not hold slots: either close the connection or count against a separate bound.
- **How long iOS keeps the exception:** only an old observation of "indefinitely". The dialog should say the warning may come back.

**For the owner:** three things only their devices and network can show: whether iOS shows the click-through and the events socket works after it, whether the cookie survives closing Safari, and whether the network lets the phone reach port 43187.

Every claim lists the search queries that were run, so a "not found" can be repeated.
